how_to_read: Each rule: dimension (policy | tone | language), severity (block = export disabled; fix = must change or attach substantiation; advisory = never blocks), sources (ids in research/regulatory_sources.md and research/brand_corpus.md), confidence (how solid the basis is). Patterns are case-insensitive JavaScript regexes run on each ad field after Minimalist product names are masked. 'provenance: downgrade' lowers severity one step when the same wording appears on the attached product page. creator_severity applies to creator/paid-partnership ads. Source ids: research/regulatory_sources.md (REG entries, OPEN-Qn = open questions for legal), research/brand_corpus.md (BRAND-§n), research/ad_corpus_notes.md (AD-CORPUS).

rules.title: Disease or drug claim
rules.rationale: A cosmetic that claims to cure, heal or treat a disease, or to kill microbes, is making a drug claim. That is outside what a cosmetic may claim in India and the US. Some conditions (cancer, leucoderma, leprosy, lupus) are on the DMR Act Schedule, which no ad may claim to prevent or cure. 'SPF 50 prevents skin cancer' is the realistic case.
rules.message: Treat / cure / heal / disease / anti-bacterial wording makes this a drug claim, which a cosmetic ad can't make.
rules.fix: Describe the cosmetic, appearance-level effect instead (e.g. 'helps reduce the look of blemishes', 'soothes the feel of dryness'). Name the ingredient and concentration rather than the condition.
rules.judge_hint: Explicit or implied treatment of a disease or medical condition, killing bacteria, healing. Includes routine-step labels like 'Treat' (flag; the reviewer may accept it as a step name).
rules.confidence: VERIFIED regulation (D&C Act s.3(b), DMR s.3 + Schedule, Meta H&W)

pass: Helps reduce the look of blemishes with 2% Salicylic Acid

rules.title: Acne / hair-fall prevention or elimination claim
rules.rationale: 'Prevents acne' or 'stops hair fall' sits on the cosmetic/drug line. Minimalist's own pages use some of this wording, so it is 'fix' with a legal question, not an automatic block.
rules.message: Preventing, clearing or fighting acne / hair fall reads as a treatment claim. It needs legal sign-off and substantiation.
rules.fix: Use appearance and feel language tied to the active: 'helps reduce the look of breakouts', 'for acne-prone skin', 'helps control excess oil'.
rules.judge_hint: Claims to prevent, stop, clear or fight acne, breakouts or hair fall, including implied ones ('say goodbye to breakouts').
rules.confidence: VERIFIED regulation, contested application — legal open question Q1

rules.title: Guarantee or absolute result
rules.rationale: No cosmetic result is guaranteed, permanent or certain for everyone. Absolute promises are misleading under ASCI Chapter I and the CCPA guidelines, and directly against Minimalist's stated 'do what they claim' position.
rules.message: A guaranteed, permanent or absolute result can't be substantiated for every user.
rules.fix: State what the product is formulated to do and what was measured, e.g. 'In-vivo tested to ISO 24444:2019 (SPF 56 measured)'. Drop 'guaranteed' / 'absolutely' / 'forever'.
rules.judge_hint: Promises of certainty, permanence or universality, including implied ones ('no more dark spots').

fail: In-vivo tested for guaranteed UV safety
pass: Leaves no visible white cast on application

rules.title: Removes / eliminates a skin concern
rules.rationale: 'Removes dark spots' or 'erases wrinkles' overstates what a cosmetic does and what the brand's own studies measured (perception and appearance over weeks).
rules.message: Removal / elimination language promises more than an appearance-level cosmetic effect.
rules.fix: Use the measured, hedged form: 'visibly reduces the appearance of dark spots', 'helps fade the look of marks'.
rules.judge_hint: Elimination verbs applied to skin concerns.

pass: Visibly reduces the appearance of dark spots

rules.title: 'Chemical-free', 'no side effects' and other safety absolutes
rules.rationale: 'Chemical-free' is false by definition (Minimalist: 'Everything is a chemical – water is a chemical'). 'No side effects' can't be substantiated for every user. Both are misleading and directly contradict the brand's founding position.
rules.message: Safety absolutes ('chemical-free', 'no side effects', '100% natural') are misleading, and Minimalist explicitly rejects this framing.
rules.fix: Say what is actually absent and verifiable: 'Fragrance free · Essential-oil free · Non-comedogenic', plus the patch-test statement.
rules.judge_hint: Safety absolutes and 'clean / natural is safe' framing, including implied ones.

pass: Fragrance free. Patch tested under dermatological supervision.

rules.title: Fairness / skin-lightening claim
rules.rationale: Fairness and whitening claims, or treating darker skin as a problem, breach ASCI's skin-lightening guidelines and are reputationally toxic in this market. 'Brighter' or 'even-looking tone' is the acceptable vocabulary.
rules.message: Fairness / whitening / skin-lightening wording is not allowed.
rules.fix: Talk about even-looking tone and the look of dark spots or pigmentation, never skin colour: 'helps even out the look of skin tone'.
rules.judge_hint: Any suggestion that lighter skin is the goal or darker skin is a problem, including 'complexion' improvements framed as lightening and before/after shade changes.
rules.confidence: VERIFIED regulation (ASCI guideline, Meta policy); scope to tan/brightening is open question Q3

fail: a potent & safe skin lightening active
pass: Helps fade the look of dark spots for a more even-looking tone

rules.title: Time-bound or instant result
rules.rationale: A result within a stated time ('in 7 days', 'overnight', 'instantly') is a specific claim. It needs a study with that duration, and the study qualifier has to be on the ad.
rules.message: A time-bound result needs a study of that duration, with the qualifier shown on the creative.
rules.fix: Keep the timeframe only if it comes from a study you can cite, and put the qualifier in the footnote (e.g. '*Consumer perception study, 4 weeks'). Otherwise remove the timeframe.
rules.judge_hint: Results promised within a time window, including 'starts working from day one'.

fail: See the change in just 28 days
pass: 90% subjects noticed visible skin clarity in 4 weeks* (*consumer perception study)

rules.title: Consumer / clinical statistic
rules.rationale: '90% subjects agreed…' is self-reported perception. It must keep that wording and carry its qualifier (what was measured, how long, ideally n) on the creative. It can't be restated as an efficacy figure.
rules.message: Statistics need their study qualifier on the creative and must not be worded more strongly than the study.
rules.fix: Quote the stat exactly as the study states it ('90% subjects said…') and add a footnote: study type (consumer perception / in-vivo / in-vitro), duration, and n if known.
rules.judge_hint: Any percentage or number describing results or users. Also check the stat isn't strengthened (perception turned into efficacy) and that a qualifier is visible.

pass: 97% subjects said skin felt less oily after 2 weeks* (*consumer perception study)

rules.title: Clinical / dermatologist authority claim
rules.rationale: 'Clinically proven' and 'dermatologist recommended' are claims of evidence or endorsement. Each needs a specific study or endorsement on file. Minimalist's pages often say 'patch tested under the supervision of a Dermatologist', which is narrower.
rules.message: Authority claims need the specific study or endorsement on file, described accurately.
rules.fix: Use the exact, narrower wording you can support, e.g. 'Patch tested for safety under the supervision of a Dermatologist', or name the test ('In-vivo SPF test, ISO 24444:2019').
rules.judge_hint: Evidence or endorsement claims: clinical, dermatologist, doctor, lab, science-proven.
rules.confidence: VERIFIED regulation; minimum study design is open question Q8

pass: Patch tested for safety under the supervision of a Dermatologist

rules.title: Regulator approval claim
rules.rationale: Regulators don't 'approve' cosmetics or testing labs. 'FDA approved' on a cosmetic is false, and 'US FDA-approved labs' implies an approval that doesn't exist.
rules.message: Regulator-approval wording is false for a cosmetic.
rules.fix: Name what actually happened, e.g. 'tested at an independent third-party lab (ISO 24444:2019)'.
rules.judge_hint: Any claim of regulator approval or certification.

fail: Clinically tested on humans in US FDA-approved labs
pass: In-vivo tested by an independent third-party lab

rules.title: Superlative or leadership claim
rules.rationale: 'Best', '#1', 'bestselling', 'India's first' need current, objective market data, and the claim's basis must be stated.
rules.message: Superlatives and rankings need objective, current substantiation, and the basis must be shown.
rules.fix: Remove it, or state the verifiable basis (source, period, category), e.g. '#1 in serums on <platform>, <month year>'.
rules.judge_hint: Comparisons with the whole market, rankings, 'best', 'most', 'only'.
rules.confidence: VERIFIED regulation; accepted data sources are open question Q9

rules.title: Comparative or disparaging claim
rules.rationale: Comparisons with other brands or 'regular' products must be fair, like-for-like and substantiated (ASCI Chapter IV), and must not disparage.
rules.message: Comparative claims need like-for-like substantiation and mustn't disparage others.
rules.fix: Drop the comparison, or state exactly what was compared and how (test, model, report number) in the footnote.
rules.judge_hint: Explicit or implied comparison with competitors, 'regular' products or alternatives (e.g. 'than neem').

fail: kills 4X more acne-causing bacteria than neem
25% more reduction than the benchmark product

rules.title: Unsourced number or social proof
rules.rationale: Factoids ('60% of skin is water'), customer counts ('300 million+ customers') and review numbers are claims too. They need a source.
rules.message: Numbers that aren't about the product's own tested results still need a source.
rules.fix: Cite the source in the footnote, or remove the number.
rules.judge_hint: Unsourced factual or statistical statements and social-proof figures.

rules.title: Asserts the viewer's condition (personal attributes)
rules.rationale: Meta's policy prohibits ads that assert or imply a viewer's personal attributes, including health or medical conditions ('Do you have acne?', 'your eczema'). Such ads get rejected or restricted.
rules.message: Addressing the viewer's own skin condition can breach Meta's personal-attributes policy.
rules.fix: Talk about the product and who it's formulated for ('for oily, acne-prone skin') instead of the viewer's condition.
rules.judge_hint: Second-person statements or questions that assert the viewer has a condition.

fail: Struggling with dark spots, acne marks, or uneven skin tone?

rules.title: Before / after or transformation framing
rules.rationale: Before/after depictions and 'transformation' framing draw platform restrictions (Meta) and need representative, unretouched evidence (ASCI).
rules.message: Before/after or transformation framing needs representative, unretouched evidence and is restricted on Meta.
rules.fix: Remove it, or use only documented, unretouched study images with their qualifier.
rules.judge_hint: Before/after imagery or wording; dramatic transformation stories.
rules.confidence: VERIFIED platform policy + ASCI; age-gating is open question Q7

rules.title: 'Free' offer without its condition
rules.rationale: A 'free' offer that depends on a purchase must state the condition clearly in the same creative (CCPA guidelines on misleading ads).
rules.message: The condition for the free item has to be in the same line or clearly next to it.
rules.fix: Put the condition right next to 'free': 'Free bottle when you buy any 2 products'.
rules.judge_hint: Free offers whose conditions are missing or hidden.

pass: Buy any 2 products and get a freebie of your choice

rules.title: Pregnancy, baby or age-safety claim
rules.rationale: 'Safe for pregnancy', 'safe for babies' and 'pediatrician approved' are high-stakes safety claims. Each needs product-specific evidence, and some Minimalist products are explicitly not recommended in pregnancy.
rules.message: Pregnancy, baby or age-safety claims need product-specific evidence and legal sign-off.
rules.fix: Only state what the product page states for this exact product, with its qualifier, or remove it.
rules.judge_hint: Safety claims for pregnancy, lactation, infants or children.
rules.confidence: VERIFIED general substantiation rule + judgment (no pregnancy-specific rule found)

rules.title: Sun-protection overclaim
rules.rationale: 'Sunblock', 'waterproof', 'sweatproof' and 'complete/100% protection' overstate what a sunscreen does. US FDA sunscreen labeling bans several of these terms, and Indian review treats them as unsubstantiated absolutes.
rules.message: Sunscreens can't claim to block everything or be waterproof. Use the tested, specific claim.
rules.fix: Use SPF/PA as tested ('Broad spectrum SPF 50, PA++++') and 'water-resistant' only if tested, plus the reapplication advice.
rules.judge_hint: Absolute sun-protection claims, waterproof/sweatproof, no need to reapply.
rules.confidence: US detail UNVERIFIED (from memory); India by analogy + ASCI enforcement focus — open question Q4

rules.title: SPF number doesn't match the product
rules.rationale: The SPF on the ad must match the product's labelled SPF exactly.
rules.message: SPF stated doesn't match the product.
rules.fix: Use the SPF printed on the pack.
rules.confidence: deterministic check against the product page / catalog

rules.title: Concentration doesn't match the product
rules.rationale: Minimalist's whole position is that the concentration on the ad is the concentration in the bottle. A strength Minimalist doesn't sell at all, or one that differs from the attached product, is a misrepresentation (raised to block after eval run 1: 'Retinol 1%' was only a fix).
rules.message: Concentration doesn't match what Minimalist sells.
rules.fix: Use the exact concentration from the pack title.
rules.confidence: deterministic check against the product page / catalog

rules.title: Individual testimonial used as a claim
rules.rationale: One customer's result ('my acne scars are almost gone') isn't substantiation, and presenting it as typical is misleading. Testimonials must be genuine, current and representative.
rules.message: A testimonial is being used as a claim.
rules.fix: Use a substantiated product claim instead, or show the testimonial clearly as one person's experience, with a 'results vary' qualifier, and only if it's genuine and on file.
rules.judge_hint: First-person customer quotes or reviews presented as product results.

rules.title: Negative statement about appearance
rules.rationale: Meta prohibits cosmetic ads that 'contain statements of inferiority about physical appearance', and ASCI 3.1(b) bars deriding people for colour, age or physical conditions.
rules.message: Attacking how someone looks (embarrassed, ugly, hide your flaws) breaches Meta's inferiority rule and the brand's tone.
rules.fix: Describe what the product does for the skin, not what's wrong with the viewer: 'Oil control that lasts all day'.
rules.judge_hint: Language that frames the viewer's appearance as bad, shameful or inferior, including about skin colour or age.

fail: Embarrassed by your oily, pore-filled face?
pass: Oil control that lasts all day

rules.title: Ingredient efficacy presented as product efficacy
rules.rationale: ASCI's 2023 beauty-category report lists 'ingredient based product efficacy claims where the product itself is not tested' as a top violation type, and EU 655/2013 says the same. This is the claim pattern a concentration-led brand is most exposed to: '10% Niacinamide is clinically proven to…' cites the ingredient's literature, not this product's test.
rules.message: A benefit proven for the ingredient is being presented as a result of this product.
rules.fix: Use 'formulated with 10% Niacinamide, an ingredient that helps…' unless there is a finished-product study, in which case cite it in the footnote.
rules.judge_hint: Efficacy, clinical or percentage claims attributed to an ingredient ('Niacinamide is clinically proven to…', 'Salicylic acid reduces acne by 50%') used as evidence that the product does it. Not raised for plain mechanism descriptions ('Salicylic acid exfoliates inside the pore').
rules.confidence: VERIFIED enforcement pattern; which SKUs have product studies is open question Q5

rules.title: Structure / function claim
rules.rationale: Claims that the product changes how the body works ('inhibits melanin production', 'boosts collagen', 'regrows hair') are drug claims in the US and fall within the DMR Act's 'structure or organic function' definition in India. That is a grey area for legal, not a regex call.
rules.message: Body structure / function wording ('inhibits melanin production', 'boosts collagen') can make a cosmetic claim a drug claim.
rules.fix: Describe the visible result instead: 'helps reduce the look of dark spots', 'helps skin look firmer'.
rules.judge_hint: Claims about changing a body process (melanin, collagen, sebum production, cell turnover, hair growth).
rules.confidence: VERIFIED definitions; India application is open question Q2

pass: helps reduce the look of dark spots

rules.title: 'New' or 'improved' claim
rules.rationale: ASCI: 'new' or 'improved' must say what is new and may be used only for one year after launch.
rules.message: 'New' / 'improved' must say what's new and is only valid for 12 months after launch.
rules.fix: Say what's new ('New: 0.1% Retinol serum') and check the launch date is within 12 months.

rules.title: Treatment wording without a named condition
rules.rationale: 'Treat' on its own ('brighten, treat, and protect', 'Step 2: Treat', 'treatment plan') positions a cosmetic as a treatment without naming a disease. The independent reviewer rated these must-fix, not block, in eval run 1; 'treats acne' style claims stay a block under CLM-01.
rules.message: 'Treat' / 'treatment' positions a cosmetic as a treatment.
rules.fix: Use a cosmetic verb: 'target', 'care for', 'help with the look of'. For routine steps, use 'Serum' or 'Step 2' instead of 'Treat'.
rules.judge_hint: Treatment vocabulary with no named condition. If a condition is named, it is CLM-01.
rules.confidence: VERIFIED definition; CDSCO 2026 notice is SECONDARY

rules.title: Vague 'clean' safety claim
rules.rationale: 'No nasties' and 'clean beauty' imply other ingredients are unsafe without saying which or why. ASCI's beauty-category report lists natural/clean claims among common violations, and EU 655 bars denigrating legally used ingredients. Narrower than CLM-05 (chemical-free, no side effects), which stays a block.
rules.message: Vague 'clean' claim: implies other ingredients are unsafe.
rules.fix: List what is actually absent and verifiable: 'Fragrance free · Essential-oil free'.

rules.title: Creator ad without paid-partnership disclosure
rules.rationale: ASCI's influencer guidelines and the CCPA endorsement rules require a clear, upfront disclosure on paid creator content.
rules.message: Creator / paid-partnership ad has no visible disclosure (#ad, Paid partnership).
rules.fix: Add '#ad' or 'Paid partnership' at the start of the caption and use the platform's paid-partnership label.

rules.title: Fear, shame or problem-agitation hook
rules.rationale: Minimalist says category marketing 'results in fear mongering', and positions itself against it. Its own copy names concerns clinically ('Acne, Oily Skin, Blackheads') rather than agitating them.
rules.message: Fear / insecurity hook: off-brand for Minimalist, which positions itself against fear-mongering.
rules.fix: Lead with the ingredient and what it does: 'Salicylic Acid 2% clears out pores' instead of 'Struggling with acne?'.
rules.judge_hint: Openers that agitate a problem or insecurity, warnings, 'say goodbye to', shame framing.

fail: Warning ⚠️ You'll stop using your old sunscreen
pass: A daily serum formulated with pure Vitamin B3 (Niacinamide) and Matmarine.

rules.title: Hype vocabulary
rules.rationale: 'No unnecessary marketing fluff' is a founding line. Brand-authored product copy has 0 instances of miracle, magic, flawless, amazing (only customer reviews use them).
rules.message: Hype word: Minimalist's own copy doesn't use it.
rules.fix: Replace it with the specific fact (ingredient, concentration, what was measured).

fail: for that flawless matt looking skin

rules.title: Emoji-led copy
rules.rationale: Brand-authored site copy has 0 emoji, and Minimalist's brand ads are nearly emoji-free. Emoji bullets are a competitor-category signature.
rules.message: Emoji-heavy copy reads like a category ad, not Minimalist.
rules.fix: Remove the emoji. Use plain line breaks for lists.

rules.title: Exclamation-heavy copy
rules.rationale: There is 1 exclamation mark in the whole Shopify description corpus. The voice is calm and declarative.
rules.message: Several exclamation marks: the brand voice is calm and declarative.
rules.fix: Use full stops.

rules.title: Urgency / scarcity pressure
rules.message: Urgency pressure isn't the brand's register (it's fine on a genuine time-bound offer, but state the dates).
rules.fix: State the offer and its real end date plainly, or drop the urgency.
rules.confidence: brand observed + regulation (dark-pattern guidance, if confirmed)

rules.title: Not educational: no ingredient or mechanism
rules.rationale: Minimalist's marketing is education-first: it names the active, the concentration and what it does. An ad with only mood words ('glow', 'radiance') and no ingredient sounds generic.
rules.message: The ad doesn't say what's in the product or how it works.
rules.fix: Name the active, its concentration and one plain-language line on what it does.
rules.judge_hint: Ads that could belong to any skincare brand: mood and outcome words with no named active, concentration or mechanism. Model-judged; only raise for brand-authored product ads (not pure offer/promo ads).

rules.title: Headline active named without its concentration
rules.rationale: 56 of 60 single products lead with a numeric strength, and the concentration is the brand's signature. Naming the hero active without its % throws that away.
rules.message: Active named without its concentration.
rules.fix: State it as on the pack: 'Niacinamide 10%'.

rules.title: Concentration written off-format
rules.rationale: Titles never put a space before % (0/49) and always write sub-1 values with a leading '0.' ('0.3%'). Leading zeros like '02%' are used inconsistently by the brand, so they're NOT enforced.
rules.message: Concentration format differs from the pack ('10%', '0.3%').
rules.fix: Write it as on the pack: no space before %, '0.3%' not '.3%'.

rules.title: 'Natural' framing
rules.rationale: Minimalist: 'the blind march towards beauty products with Natural claims is really concerning'. The brand sells on actives, not on naturalness.
rules.message: 'Natural' framing runs against the brand's stated position.
rules.fix: Name the actual ingredient and its function instead.

rules.title: Unhedged efficacy where the brand hedges
rules.rationale: Brand copy scopes efficacy to appearance and feel ('visibly reduces the appearance of', 'helps', 'even-looking'). Unhedged mechanism-free outcome verbs read as generic category copy.
rules.message: Outcome stated more strongly than the brand's usual appearance-level wording.
rules.fix: Scope it: 'visibly', 'the look of', 'helps'.
rules.judge_hint: Outcome verbs (brightens, fades, evens, transforms, fixes) with no 'visibly / helps / appearance' scoping. Only raise when clearly unhedged; don't flag mechanism statements like 'Niacinamide reduces sebum'.
rules.confidence: brand observed (mixed evidence: the brand is itself inconsistent)

rules.title: Vague purity claim
rules.rationale: Minimalist states purity precisely ('86% pure Vitamin C content', named supplier grades). '100% pure' is the category's vague version.
rules.message: Vague purity claim: state the grade or source as the product page does.
rules.fix: Use the page's precise wording, e.g. 'Ethyl Ascorbic Acid, 86% pure Vitamin C content'.
